content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors proposed a regularizer (DAIR) that penalize the difference between the model performance on original data and augmented data. The authors argued that the new regularizer imposes invariance and effectively prevented the model from overfitting to spurious features. By applying the regularizer on various types of machine learning tasks, the authors analyzed the experiments results and explained the empirical novelty.
content.main_review:
The authors proposed a regularizer to further improve the effectiveness of utilizing augmented data. Great amount of experiments are conducted to demonstrate the impact of DAIR. Overall the idea is simple and clean.

Here are some major concerns:
1. The authors proposed the new regularizer to reduce the effect of spurious features. There should be some works have discussed upon this topic other than data augmentation. For example, self-training work [1]. Dropout could be another method that can help upon this purpose. The author should involve such work for analysis or comparison.
2. The regularizer proposed requires a one to one corresponding between original samples and augmented samples. However, many data augmentation method could not provide such augmented data, e.g. mixup. This requires strong prior knowledge about the spurious feature and the distribution shift, thus limited the usage of the proposed method.
3. The idea of penalizing the performance difference on original data and augmented data is not quite original. For example, some works in multi-view tasks have proposed to penalize the difference between logits of multiple views for the same entity. Though not proposed for exactly the same purpose, and similar ideas could be encouraged as long as it is reasonable and works. However, this could still weaken the originality and novelty of the proposed idea in this paper.
4. This might be a minor point. The demo experiment in section 2.1 is not really convincing. The author proposed a rare scenario that one feature will only available at training time.  The setting looks like being specifically manipulated to benefit the proposed method. 

[1] Chen, Y., Wei, C., Kumar, A. and Ma, T. Self-training avoids using spurious features under domain shift. NeurIPS 2020

Moreover, the originality and novelty of the idea is not strong. These lead to my current conclusion: The is paper is marginally below the acceptance threshold.

content.title: Official Response to Reviewer 5h6n
content.comment:
*The authors proposed the new regularizer to reduce the effect of spurious features. There should be some works have discussed upon this topic other than data augmentation. For example, self-training work [1]. Dropout could be another method that can help upon this purpose. The author should involve such work for analysis or comparison.*

We thank the reviewer for bringing this up. We expanded our literature survey to discuss the existing works on consistency regularization. In particular, we revised Sections 1 and 2 to better position DAIR, which promotes loss consistency, as opposed to the existing literature on consistency regularization that targets feature consistency in general. The loss consistency through DAIR is applicable when pairing information is available between original and augmented samples (image example: augmented sample is a rotation of the original sample; language example: augmented sample is the original sample with named entities replaced from a different bank). On the other hand, DAIR would not be applicable in some other setups such as DomainBed (Gulrajani & Lopez-Paz, ICLR 2020) where such pairing information is not available. 

In this paper, we show through extensive experiments that DAIR framework is still broadly applicable to many real-world setups and leads to significant performance boost in very different experimental setups (namely robust regression against spurious features and label noise, invariant question answering, training robust neural networks against adversarial attacks, and neural task-oriented dialog modeling), and have compared the performance with strong baselines for each task. Note that we are not aware of the existing works on consistency regularization that would outright apply to all these setups, e.g., regression or generative models, that we have used for experiments in Section 3. If we have missed important baselines, we appreciate it if the reviewer can explicitly point us to them so that we can include them in our comparisons.

====================

*The regularizer proposed requires a one to one corresponding between original samples and augmented samples. However, many data augmentation method could not provide such augmented data, e.g. mixup. This requires strong prior knowledge about the spurious feature and the distribution shift, thus limited the usage of the proposed method.*

Thank you for this comment. Your point is completely valid; and this can be viewed as a limitation of DAIR as it is only applicable when we have “pairing” information between a sample and its augmented variant. We make this clear in Sections 1 and 2 in the revised paper. Having said that, we respectfully disagree that the usage of the proposed method is limited, as there are a variety of applications where such pairing information is available and DAIR can exploit such information. We show four such real-world benchmarks in Section 3 to validate this, where we show that DAIR outperforms strong baselines for these problems.

====================

*The idea of penalizing the performance difference on original data and augmented data is not quite original. For example, some works in multi-view tasks have proposed to penalize the difference between logits of multiple views for the same entity. Though not proposed for exactly the same purpose, and similar ideas could be encouraged as long as it is reasonable and works. However, this could still weaken the originality and novelty of the proposed idea in this paper.*

We agree with the reviewer that consistency regularization is not new; and we make this point clear in the introduction. We tried to make the literature survey more comprehensive and credit the existing literature. We also appreciate it if you can please point out any other missing references so that we can complete the literature review. However, to the best of our knowledge loss consistency is relatively unexplored and DAIR-SQ has not been proposed before. We show that this simple regularization can lead to significant boosts in a variety of problem setups.

====================

*This might be a minor point. The demo experiment in section 2.1 is not really convincing. The author proposed a rare scenario that one feature will only available at training time. The setting looks like being specifically manipulated to benefit the proposed method.*

The purpose of Section 2.1 is to provide a toy example showing that the performance of DA-ERM is fundamentally limited (even in the limit of infinite data) whereas with proper regularization for consistency of loss functions one can achieve much better (or even optimal) generalization. Hence, the gain of regularization is not in just better sample complexity, but rather it can be fundamentally learning better models. We have revised Section 2.1 to make the point more clear.

====================

[1] Chen, Y., Wei, C., Kumar, A. and Ma, T. Self-training avoids using spurious features under domain shift. NeurIPS 2020

replying_to: Replying to DAIR: Data Augmented Invariant Regularization
display_title: Official Review of Paper253 by Reviewer zaca

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies a new learning method that makes a model be invariant under a data augmentation (implicitly, to achieve high test performance when the test data distribution is different from the training data distribution). The authors propose a new objective function, called DAIR, characterized by a regularized function where a regularizer maintains the performance of the model on data augmentations. Some numerical experiments by varying regularizers and datasets are provided (in Sections 2 and 3), and some theoretical results are presented. The authors claim that DAIR consistently outperforms the baseline methods including ERM and DA-ERM.
content.main_review:
Main comments:
- The form of a new regularization function in DAIR is reasonable but requires prior knowledge of data augmentation functions. This can be a critical drawback of this method, especially when a distribution of augmented data is quite different from a test data distribution. As far as the reviewer understands, most of the theoretical and experimental results presented in this paper implicitly assume that data augmentation functions are designed to cover the test data distribution or the like. For instance, in the rotated MNIST experiment in Section 2.2, ERM (without data augmentation) is compared with DAIR (with weak rotation) when the test set consists of 'strong rotation' samples. In that sense, the good performance of DAIR is not surprising. 
- In applications, it might be challenging (or even impossible) to consider a 'good' data augmentation technique for future test datasets. Maybe the authors need to perform sensitivity analyses to see the effect of misspecification of data augmentations on test performance. For example, what if 'weak rotation samples' are augmented but the test dataset consists of location-shifted images? 

Theoretical results:
- All the results are too restrictive. Proposition 1 considers a very specific setup (a linear model $y=x+\epsilon$ and a data augmentation $A(z)=(x, ay+n)$). I do not think the theoretical result is wrong, but it is difficult to imagine an extension to more general settings (e.g. non-linear models or different augmentations). Also, the current result considers the infinity lambda case, which is basically designed for the test distribution. 
- Lemma 1 is rather straightforward and only compares DAIR-SQ and DAIR-L1. What if we consider the other regularization functions?

Experiment results:
- As the authors mentioned in the paper, the comparison with IRM might not be fair as IRM does not use augmentation samples. Is there a fair baseline for this experiment?

Minors:
- In the first paragraph of section 3.1: 'by by' -> 'by'
- In the first paragraph of appendix D: 'is is' -> 'is'
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a new objective function to train a model that is invariant under data augmentations. It seems the goal of this paper makes sense, but the theoretical and experimental results are too restrictive to consider various settings.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.title: Official Response to Reviewer zaca - Part I
content.comment:
*The form of a new regularization function in DAIR is reasonable but requires prior knowledge of data augmentation functions. This can be a critical drawback of this method, especially when a distribution of augmented data is quite different from a test data distribution. As far as the reviewer understands, most of the theoretical and experimental results presented in this paper implicitly assume that data augmentation functions are designed to cover the test data distribution or the like. For instance, in the rotated MNIST experiment in Section 2.2, ERM (without data augmentation) is compared with DAIR (with weak rotation) when the test set consists of 'strong rotation' samples. In that sense, the good performance of DAIR is not surprising.*

As the reviewer points out when the data augmentation is done via strong rotation and testing is also done with strong rotation, DA-ERM seems to work well; however as we observed here, when the data augmentation scheme is weak rotation, DA-ERM does not generalize well to strong rotation. We observe here that DAIR helps to close this gap.

We also agree with the reviewer that designing good data augmentation functions is a hard task in general. Nevertheless data augmentation remains a core principle in machine learning for solving various supervised/unsupervised/self-supervised tasks. Our proposal doesn't solve the difficulty of devising good data augmentation procedures; rather we argue that if we are already performing data augmentation to generate samples that are believed to require consistent performance with respect to the original ones, DAIR can do even better (almost) for free via further regularization of the losses and leads to non-trivial  performance boost. 

Regarding your comment  that  *data augmentation functions are designed to cover the test data distribution or the like*, we would like to remark that in the dialog state tracking experiment (Section 3.4 of the revised paper), our data augmentation scheme is to scramble a named entity (e.g., “cambridge” -> “bdemcgria”). On the other hand, the test-time distribution involves replacing the UK named entities with US ones (e.g., “cambridge” -> “san francisco”). While arguably the data augmentation does still capture the essence of the distribution shift around changing of the named entities, designing data augmentation techniques that can generalize to *any* test-time distribution shift is beyond the scope of this paper.

====================

*In applications, it might be challenging (or even impossible) to consider a 'good' data augmentation technique for future test datasets. Maybe the authors need to perform sensitivity analyses to see the effect of misspecification of data augmentations on test performance. For example, what if 'weak rotation samples' are augmented but the test dataset consists of location-shifted images?*


While we agree with the reviewer that designing general-purpose data augmentation schemes is an important task, our proposal is a regularizer that is applicable whenever data augmentation is used for consistency. We validate this claim through several real-world benchmarks in Section 3, where DAIR sets new state-of-the-art results in important practical problems. 

====================

*All the results are too restrictive. Proposition 1 considers a very specific setup (a linear model $y=x+\epsilon$ and a data augmentation $A(z)=(x,ay+n))$. I do not think the theoretical result is wrong, but it is difficult to imagine an extension to more general settings (e.g. non-linear models or different augmentations). Also, the current result considers the infinity lambda case, which is basically designed for the test distribution.*

The purpose of section 2.1 is not to develop theory for consistency regularization but rather to provide a toy example showing that the performance of DA-ERM is fundamentally limited. The goal of this simple exercise was to show that there are cases where data augmentation is fundamentally limited whereas with proper regularization for consistency of loss functions one can achieve much improved generalization (even if the number of samples can be infinite). Hence, the gain of regularization is not in just better sample complexity, but rather it can be fundamentally learning better models. While we agree with the reviewer that $\lambda \to \infty$ is a limitation of this analysis, Figure 1 uses $\lambda = 100$ to solve DAIR.

content.title: Official Response to Reviewer zaca - Part II
content.comment:
====================

*Lemma 1 is rather straightforward and only compares DAIR-SQ and DAIR-L1. What if we consider the other regularization functions?*

DAIR regularization is applied at the very last layer (i.e., directly the loss function). As such, we compared the two variants, DAIR-L1 and DAIR-SQ head to head to understand why DAIR-SQ works significantly better in practice, especially in problems involving non-convex models (such as CNNs in this case). This is the reason that we only consider DAIR-SQ and DAIR-L1 for comparison. Other consistency regularization variants cannot be directly applied to regression and generative models (two of our main experiments in Section 3). Finally, we would like to emphasize that the aim of Lemma 1 is to provide intuition on the advantage of using DAIR-SQ. We included more details in the revised manuscript on the benefit of DAIR in Section 2.3.

====================

*As the authors mentioned in the paper, the comparison with IRM might not be fair as IRM does not use augmentation samples. Is there a fair baseline for this experiment?*

We agree that it might not be a fair comparison but we believe IRM still serves as a baseline. IRM aims at enforcing environment/group-level consistency in the model. In contrast, our work “pairs” the data points and exploits this pairing information during training (when available). While this means that DAIR requires this pairing information (which can be viewed as a limitation), as we demonstrated in our experiments, exploiting this pairing information can significantly boost the performance of the trained model when such information is available.

We also remark that in the real-world experiments in Section 3, we use strong state-of-the-art baselines and show that DAIR outperforms them by exploiting the loss consistency between the original and augmented examples.


====================

*In the first paragraph of section 3.1: 'by by' -> 'by'*
*In the first paragraph of appendix D: 'is is' -> 'is'*

Thank you for pointing out these typos. We corrected the typos in the revised paper.


====================

*This paper proposes a new objective function to train a model that is invariant under data augmentations. It seems the goal of this paper makes sense, but the theoretical and experimental results are too restrictive to consider various settings.*

We respectfully disagree with the reviewer that the experimental results are too restrictive to consider various settings. We have considered four real-world experimental setups with various modeling strategies and established the effectiveness of DAIR through these setups, and have compared DAIR with strong baselines for each of the respective problems.

Although the authors mentioned "designing good data augmentation functions is a hard task in general", the lack of extensive analysis of misspecified settings is a major weakness of this paper. replying_to: Replying to Thank you for responses

content.title: Thanks for your response
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer for taking time to read our responses, read the revised paper, and write a response to us. We really appreciate it. We also thank the reviewer for acknowledging the potential and interesting insights in the revised paper.

We agree with the reviewer that *[DAIR] can completely fail if a pre-defined data augmentation is misspecified,* and it may not generalize if the nature of the distribution shift completely changes at test time, e.g., data augmentation used for color at training time but the digits are rotated at test time. While we have not tested this, we have no reason to believe that vanilla data augmentation or DAIR would help in this situation. We also agree with the reviewer that generalization to unseen distribution shifts is an extremely important problem in domain generalization that is actively being tackled by our community, and DAIR is not (directly) solving it. We also agree with the reviewer that it remains to be seen whether DAIR could be a useful component in solving the main domain generalization (to unseen distribution shifts) problem.

Having said that, "data augmentation engineering" is still a core principle in solving many practical machine learning problems, and for three of the major baselines we improve upon (published in ICML 2019, CVPR 2020, and NeurIPS 2020), the state-of-the-art solution is built via data augmentation engineering. For example, generating adversarial examples and adding them to training set remains a main direction in achieving robustness to adversarial attacks; augmenting training data with invariant training examples was the method that resulted in the previous state-of-the-art performance on the visual question answering; data augmentation with named entity scrambling resulted in state-of-the-art performance with respect to the named entity memorization problem in dialog state tracking. What DAIR currently brings to the table is: If you are using data augmentation engineering to solve a practical problem, you can improve upon it via a simple regularization that has proved to be effective and robust on a variety of tasks and model architectures. 

Given that "data augmentation engineering" is widespread in practical machine learning, we argue that DAIR makes a useful contribution for practitioners albeit it doesn't solve the domain generalization problem to unseen distribution shifts as rightly argued by the reviewer. Our disagreement with the reviewer is simply on whether this is sufficient contribution for our paper to be accepted at ICLR; and we respect the reviewer's opinion to the contrary.

Thanks, 
\
Authors
\
\
\
**References**

H. Zhang, Y. Yu, J. Jiao, E. Xing, L. E. Ghaoui, and M. Jordan. "Theoretically principled trade-off between robustness
and accuracy." *ICML 2019* (https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08573).

Vedika Agarwal, Rakshith Shetty, and Mario Fritz. "Towards causal VQA: Revealing and reducing spurious correlations by invariant and covariant semantic editing." *CVPR 2020* (https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.07538).

Ehsan Hosseini-Asl, Bryan McCann, Chien-Sheng Wu, Semih Yavuz, and Richard Socher. "A simple language model for task-oriented dialogue." *NeurIPS 2020* (https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00796).

replying_to: Replying to DAIR: Data Augmented Invariant Regularization
display_title: Official Review of Paper253 by Reviewer VMQe

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a conceptually simple regularizer which forces consistency of loss between the true samples and their corresponding augmentations, termed DAIR-SQ. The authors demonstrate the qualitative characteristics of DAIR-SQ with a clean toy example, and a supporting theoretical result of asymptotic consistency on the same. For real-world datasets, the authors demonstrate the robustness induced by DAIR-SQ under domain shift, label noise, and adversarial attacks.
content.main_review:
### Strengths

- The proposed regularizer is conceptually simple and a natural consequence of what we expect from the training.
- The authors present a very clean and simple toy problem to ease the reader into qualitative characteristics of DAIR-SQ.
- The authors have made a conscious effort in framing the flow of the paper while writing, which is much appreciated. It is well-written.

### Weaknesses

- While the toy example is well-scoped, I am a little concerned about the setup here, making it unfair for (DA-)ERM. It is a little stretch to consider unregularized ERM, an unreasonably weakened baseline. In practice too, I presume one would typically apply regularization via weight decay. There is no reason for ERM to do anything better because the space of possible functions hasn't been constrained in line with our expectations anyways, effectively causing overfitting.
- The usual parameter regularization also generally appears to be absent for any description in the paper. Is that just assumed to be obviously a part of the system?
- Does Figure 2 contradict Proposition 1? Figure 2 says that there is a sweet spot for $\lambda$? Or is it the fact that we only have a finite sample?
- What explains the characteristic bump in Figure 2 for DAIR-SQ and some other variants? I think these graphs show there is a setting of $\lambda$ for which DAIR-SQ would outperform others, but I am still unsure the conditions under which this happens.
- Perhaps it is implicit in the existing results, but is it possible to visualize whether DAIR-SQ *really* adds invariance? For instance, it seems unreasonable to believe that a "6" changing into "9" should remain invariant. To that end, I am not sure why Strong Rotations are even meaningful to be checked. It it possible to visualize a sequence of rotations of say "6" and see where (DA-)ERM breaks versus DAIR-SQ?
- For the unsupervised learning setup, I am still unsure why we couldn't add a regularizer for $g$ such that we force $g(f(x;\theta_1);\theta_2) \approx g(f(\widetilde{x};\theta_1);\theta_2)$ via $\mathcal{R}_2$? (We could potentially freeze $\theta_1$ in this case since we already have another regularization term that handles that). Could the authors expand on this?
- I am not sure how much to trust Figure 7 to validate the fact that $\mathcal{R}_2$ forces the same distributions. There could be more high variance directions just not covered in the first two dimensions. How does the eigenspectrum look like?
- Would it be correct to say that Proposition 1 remains limited to the very specific 2-D case? Or can the proof be extended to more general versions? If not, then it is unclear to me what to take away from the theoretical justification.

### Minor Comments

- A labeled Figure 1 would make things easier for the reader. The caption is also not informative, perhaps the parameters don't matter for the intuitive story being told here.
- The authors mentioned the regularizer $\mathcal{R}$ to be a proper divergence in passing but most of the description of considering unnormalized NLL seems unnecessary since the actual regularizer used does not have an immediate direct likelihood interpretation. Please let me know if I am missing something obvious. (could have been a Gaussian centered at either the sample or its augmented version if not for the square root factor)
content.summary_of_the_review: The method obviously seems to work and the authors do a good job of taking a varied set of problems to demonstrate effectiveness. The proposed method is conceptually simple, and therefore most of my concerns lie with the experimental justifications as highlighted in the main review.

display_title: Official Response to Reviewer VMQe - Part I

content.title: Official Response to Reviewer VMQe - Part I
content.comment:
*While the toy example is well-scoped, I am a little concerned about the setup here, making it unfair for (DA-)ERM. It is a little stretch to consider unregularized ERM, an unreasonably weakened baseline. In practice too, I presume one would typically apply regularization via weight decay. There is no reason for ERM to do anything better because the space of possible functions hasn't been constrained in line with our expectations anyways, effectively causing overfitting.*

The purpose of Section 2.1 is to provide a toy example, in which the improvements offered by DA-ERM are limited even when we have infinite samples ($n \to \infty$), whereas DAIR can recover optimal performance. We agree with the reviewer that ERM is not a good baseline in this setup, as it converges to a very bad solution (by design). We revised Section 2.1 to motivate it better and added a brief conclusion at the end of Section 2.1 to conclude that the improvements by DAIR are not simply limited to better sample complexity. 


Also, it is not hard to see that even a weight decay regularizer would not result in choosing the correct feature in this example, as the ERM solution, i.e., $(0,1)$ does not suffer from the usual sense of overfitting (large weight). We formally prove this in Proposition 2 in Appendix A (page 15). While this is just a toy example to motivate DAIR, we further evaluated the practical performance of DAIR in later sections of the paper. In particular, we compared DAIR with various algorithms (including IRM, DRO, REx in Table 13, page 21, Appendix E in the revised paper) designed specifically for imposing invariance in several benchmarks. We caution, however, that this comparison is not quite apples to apples as DAIR exploits the pairing information between samples and augmented samples.


====================

*The usual parameter regularization also generally appears to be absent for any description in the paper. Is that just assumed to be obviously a part of the system?*

No extra parameter regularization is used in experiments involving DAIR whereas some of the baselines in real-world experiments have regularizers baked in. While parameter regularization can help avoid overfitting in the absence of sufficient training data points, it will not necessarily result in invariant models. This fact can be seen in the toy example where even with an infinite number of training data points, weight decay regularizer could not reach the performance of DAIR (see Proposition 2 in Appendix A, Page 15).

====================

*Does Figure 2 contradict Proposition 1? Figure 2 says that there is a sweet spot for $\lambda$? Or is it the fact that we only have a finite sample?*

We thank the reviewer for this question as it prompted us to dig deeper into the reasons for the characteristic bump in Figure 2. As we now explain in Appendix B (Page 16) we identified three potential explanations for this sweet spot: 

- We observed that a large $\lambda$ requires a relatively longer time for convergence. This is in line with the classical results in the optimization literature where larger Lipschitz constants (resulting from adding a regularizer) slows down the convergence rate. Thus, as we are training all models for a certain number of epochs, we will end up with underfitting. We added Appendix B to further discuss this effect.

- A larger $\lambda$ is more likely to guide the optimization trajectory towards a spurious poor local minimum with poor performance. We have experimentally verified this in Section 2.3 (Figure 6, Page 6) as the reason for the poor performance of DAIR-L1.

- In addition, as pointed out by the reviewer, with a finite number of samples our regularizer does not necessarily lead to the best possible performance in the infinite sample setting (with weak domain shift). Hence, we might expect to observe the classical approximation-estimation tradeoff. This is especially true in real-world scenarios where one might expect that the difficulty of the example may not necessarily be preserved through data augmentation, and hence forcing the loss to be equal on both samples might be detrimental to the overall performance, which may lead to a practical sweet spot for $\lambda$ (e.g., Fig 8 and Table 16). 


====================

*What explains the characteristic bump in Figure 2 for DAIR-SQ and some other variants? I think these graphs show there is a setting of $\lambda$ for which DAIR-SQ would outperform others, but I am still unsure the conditions under which this happens.*

The bump in Figure 2 for DAIR-SQ and other variants can be explained by the reasons discussed above (response to the reviewer’s previous question). The goal of the experiments in Section 2.2 is to show that DAIR-SQ is relatively stable across different settings with practical constraints on the number of training epochs, learning rates, etc. Please see Appendix B (Page 16-17) for the justifications around the sweet spot performance for $\lambda$.

content.comment:
====================

*Perhaps it is implicit in the existing results, but is it possible to visualize whether DAIR-SQ really adds invariance? For instance, it seems unreasonable to believe that a "6" changing into "9" should remain invariant. To that end, I am not sure why Strong Rotations are even meaningful to be checked. It it possible to visualize a sequence of rotations of say "6" and see where (DA-)ERM breaks versus DAIR-SQ?*

Thank you for your suggestion based on which we introduced the consistency metric at the beginning of Section 2, and will report it in the experiments.  While some of the experiments are still running, we observe significant boosts in consistency. For example, on joint goal accuracy in neural dialog modeling (Table 4 of Section 3.4 in revised paper), we observe more than 5% boost in consistency compared to DA-ERM. Table 2 (Section 3.2) also shows that consistency of the VQA models are improved by adding the DAIR regularizer. 

Additionally, we also specifically explored consistency on digits for Rotated MNIST to check consistency with respect to digits 6 and 9 to 180$^\circ$ rotation (Table 15, page 22). We observe that digits 6 and 9 are challenging to get right (as one would expect for them to be difficult to tell apart). While we see 2−3% drop on the consistency for digits 6 and 9 (when rotating them by 180$^\circ$),the drop is smaller than expected perhaps due to the fact that the CNN learns to classify these digits based on features that are different from those of humans. 


====================

*For the unsupervised learning setup, I am still unsure why we couldn't add a regularizer for $g$ such that we force $g(f(x;\theta_1);\theta_2)\simeq g(f(\widetilde{x};\theta_1);\theta_2)$ via $\mathcal{R}_2$? (We could potentially freeze $\theta_1$ in this case since we already have another regularization term that handles that). Could the authors expand on this?*

In this experiment, forcing $g(f(x;\theta_1);\theta_2)\simeq g(f(\widetilde{x};\theta_1);\theta_2)$ would not work because if we have a perfect autoencoder with 0 loss for every input sample, the color information may (will) still be perfectly retained in the embedding. We agree with the reviewers that Section 3.4 was poorly connected with the rest of the paper. Hence, we decided to remove this section in our revised paper. Instead, we included more discussions on DAIR and its motivation. We also included additional experiments on dialog state tracking to demonstrate the benefits of loss inconsistency regularization (Section 3.4 of the revised paper).

====================

*I am not sure how much to trust Figure 7 to validate the fact that R2 forces the same distributions. There could be more high variance directions just not covered in the first two dimensions. How does the eigenspectrum look like?*

As explained above, we decided to remove Section 3.4 following your comment (and Reviewer hj8W’s comment).

====================

*Would it be correct to say that Proposition 1 remains limited to the very specific 2-D case? Or can the proof be extended to more general versions? If not, then it is unclear to me what to take away from the theoretical justification.*

The purpose of Section 2.1 is not to develop theory but rather providing a toy example showing that the performance of DA-ERM is limited even in the limit of infinite samples and DAIR can provide a fundamental improvement over DA-ERM. While we think it is possible to extend the setup beyond two features, we believe that would not add much value to the narrative of the paper as the problem remains a toy example and the conclusion remains the same: DA-ERM is not sufficient to enforce consistency of performance on augmented samples. We revised Section 2.1 to motivate the example better and added a brief conclusion at the end of Section 2.1.  We also included Proposition 2 in Appendix A to illustrate that DA-ERM cannot recover the optimal classifier even in the presence of a data-independent weight-decay regularizer.

====================

*A labeled Figure 1 would make things easier for the reader. The caption is also not informative, perhaps the parameters don't matter for the intuitive story being told here.*

We revised accordingly.

====================

*The authors mentioned the regularizer $\mathcal{R}$ to be a proper divergence in passing but most of the description of considering unnormalized NLL seems unnecessary since the actual regularizer used does not have an immediate direct likelihood interpretation. Please let me know if I am missing something obvious. (could have been a Gaussian centered at either the sample or its augmented version if not for the square root factor)*

This discussion was needed to define the other forms of consistency regularization in Section 2.2, such as KL-divergence and L2 consistency regularization. As such, we moved it to the beginning of Section 2.2 to avoid confusion and updated the exposure of DAIR in Section 2.1.

content.title: Official Response to Reviewer hj8W - Part I
content.comment:
*The importance of loss inconsistency is not well described. What is the advantage of loss inconsistency compared with feature inconsistency loss in self-supervised learning?*

Thanks for this question, based on which we have revised Sections 1 and 2 to better position our proposal. We recap these updates here to respond as well. We focus on the loss consistency, which could be viewed as a special case of feature consistency at the very last layer (assuming loss to be a layer of its own). As loss could usually be viewed as the log likelihood of the sample under the model, loss consistency enforces $P(\text{label} | \text{features})$ to be the same on both the original and augmented examples. Note that loss consistency is a relatively weaker requirement compared to feature consistency. However, it requires pairing information between the two samples, i.e., the expectation of similar performance on an augmented sample and an original one, which might be viewed as a limitation of our framework as it won’t apply to setups such as DomainBed (Gulrajani & Lopez-Paz, ICLR 2020). Having said that, we argue that this weaker form of consistency is suitable for problems where feature consistency may not be conceptually meaningful. For instance, in language modeling when a pair of sentences  differ in their corresponding named entities, it is not clear why we should enforce their embeddings to be similar, however, loss consistency is still meaningful promoting the probability of label given input to be the same on the original and the augmented samples. We can see how this is applied in the new Section 3.4 on neural dialog modeling. 

====================

*In 3p, there are SQ regularize, square root of loss inconsistency, but the intuition of square is not well discussed.*

The intuition of the square here is to make the scaling of the regularizer the same as the loss function itself, which in turn makes the tuning procedure easier from an optimization perspective. For example, if the loss function is multiplied by a constant, then the learner does not need to re-tune the optimal $\lambda$ value. This would simplify the tuning procedure of DAIR for different tasks and even different loss functions. Empirically we observed that optimal $\lambda$ is ~10 for robust regression, ~1 for invariant VQA, ~10 for adversarially robust deep learning, ~0.5 for the task-oriented dialog experiment, while these tasks have very different losses and network architectures. In addition, $\mathcal{R}_{\text{sq}} = (\sqrt {\ell (z;\theta)} - \sqrt{\ell(\widetilde{z};\theta)})^2$ is differentiable as long as the loss is strictly positive which helps with optimization procedure. This would not remain true if we replace the square with absolute value. 

====================

*In section 3.4, this paper adopts feature regularization, instead of loss inconsistency. It is hard to understand the reason.*

We agree with the reviewer that Section 3.4 of the original submission was poorly matched to the proposal of the paper. As we focus this paper’s contribution on loss consistency, we decided to remove this section in our revised paper and replace it with a generative model for dialog state tracking in task-oriented dialog systems where DAIR-SQ is applied. We also used some of the opened up space to add more discussions on DAIR and its motivation to satisfy reviewers’ comments in Sections 1 and 2.

====================

*For section 3.4, What is the advantage of DAIR compared with [1].*

As discussed above, we decided to remove section 3.4 of the original submission. We have added discussion around the differences between loss consistency and feature consistency in the introduction.

====================

*There are many related works for learning invariant feature representation [2,3,4], and some of the works can be interpreted as loss inconsistency regularization research. What is the advantage of DAIR compared with [2,3,4]?*

We thank the reviewer for bringing up the works [2,3,4]. These three works aim at enforcing environment/group-level consistency to the model. In contrast, our work “pairs” the data points and exploits this pairing information during training. While this means that DAIR requires this additional pairing information (which can be viewed as a limitation), as we demonstrated in our experiments, exploiting this pairing information (when available) can significantly boost the performance of the trained model. In particular, we compare DAIR with [2,3,4] on Colored MNIST (see Table 13, page 21, Appendix E in the revised paper), where we show that DAIR outperforms [2,3,4]. In short, here are the results: DRO: 37.40, IRM: 66.90, REx: 68.70, DAIR: 72.58. However, we caution that the baselines do not need/use the pairing information that DAIR uses, so this comparison is not quite apples to apples.

content.title: General response to all reviewers & summary of revisions
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and extensive comments and feedback, which has helped us significantly improve the paper. We apologize for posting our response towards the end of the discussion period as we wanted to make sure we responded to all comments point by point and comprehensively. As a result, we have made several revisions to the paper with new experiments, and discussions based on the reviewers’ feedback as outlined below. We also clarified the positioning of this paper with respect to the existing body of literature in terms of novelty, applicability, and limitations. Finally, we also posted point-by-point responses to the specific questions/comments by all reviewers.

- We revised Sections 1 and 2 to better position DAIR, which promotes loss consistency, as opposed to the existing literature on consistency regularization that targets feature consistency in general. The loss consistency through DAIR is applicable when pairing information is available between original and augmented samples (image example: augmented sample is a rotation of the original sample; language example: augmented sample is the original sample with named entities replaced from a different bank). On the other hand, DAIR would not be applicable in some other setups such as DomainBed (Gulrajani & Lopez-Paz, ICLR 2020) where such pairing information is not available. Having said that, we argue that this weaker form of consistency is suitable for problems where feature consistency may not be conceptually meaningful. For instance, in language modeling when a pair of sentences differ in their corresponding named entities, it is not clear why we should enforce their embeddings to be similar, however, loss consistency is still meaningful promoting the probability of label given input to be the same on the original and the augmented samples. In this paper, we show through extensive experiments that this framework is still broadly applicable to many real-world setups and leads to significant performance boost in very different experimental setups (namely robust regression against spurious features and label noise, invariant visual question answering, training robust neural networks against adversarial attacks, and neural task-oriented dialog modeling). Thanks to the reviewers, we also *included several missing pointers* that the reviewers mentioned and other ones that we felt would clarify the positioning of the paper. 

- Reviewers raised concerns about Section 3.4 (unsupervised learning using autoencoders) in the original paper being a poor match to the proposal of the paper. We agree with the reviewers and removed this section/experiment and replaced it with a *dialog state tracking* task in task-oriented dialog using neural generative models. We believe that this additional experiment, in which DAIR outperforms a strong baseline, called SimpleTOD (Hosseini-Asl et al., NeurIPS 2020), better justifies the broad applicability of DAIR to real-world problems.

- To empirically justify that loss consistency results in the consistency of performance, we defined a consistency metric in Section 2.1 that is applicable to any 0-1 performance metric (e.g., accuracy in classification or joint goal accuracy in dialog state tracking), and we plan to report the consistency metric for all experiments as well. While we have not obtained the results for one of the experiments yet (will be added to the paper later), we demonstrate *significant boosts in the consistency metric* as a result of loss consistency regularization via DAIR in real-world experiments.

We thank the reviewers again for their constructive feedback, and we hope that the reviewers find our revisions and responses satisfactory in making their final judgement of our paper!

Sincerely,

Authors of Paper 253

 
 

**References**

Ishaan Gulrajani and David Lopez-Paz. In search of lost domain generalization. ICLR, 2020.

Ehsan Hosseini-Asl, Bryan McCann, Chien-Sheng Wu, Semih Yavuz, and Richard Socher. A simple language model for task-oriented dialogue. NeurIPS, 2020.
